messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi had always been drawn to the fast-paced world of urban planning, but after the assault six months ago, every crowded street and chaotic construction site seemed to hold a new menace. The smell of alcohol, which used to remind him of college parties, now transported him back to that night. Even the sound of objects being thrown or people expressing anger calmly made his heart rate spike. These triggers had become ubiquitous in his daily life as an urban planner, and Kofi found himself avoiding certain projects or meetings, fearing he might be confronted with one of these stimuli. As a result, Kofi began to ruminate on what he could have done differently that night, dwelling on self-blame. He became convinced that if only he had been more assertive or vigilant, the assault wouldn't have happened. This self-doubt seeped into other areas of his life, making him question his ability to cope with even minor setbacks. He started to feel helpless, as if bad things were bound to happen to him no matter what he did. Kofi's colleagues noticed a change in him; he became more withdrawn and hesitant to take on new challenges. To distract himself from these feelings of inadequacy, Kofi turned to gambling. He would spend hours online, trying to win back the sense of control he felt he had lost. But even as he gambled, he couldn't shake off the feeling that he was in danger. Every sudden sound or movement made him jump, and he found himself constantly scanning his surroundings for potential threats. Kofi's memories of the assault were fragmented, consisting of vivid snapshots: the sound of shattering glass, the feel of pavement beneath his face, and the smell of alcohol wafting through the air. When these memories resurfaced, Kofi felt overwhelmed by emotion, unable to articulate what had happened. He would try to describe the events to friends or family, but the words got stuck in his throat. As he struggled to make sense of his experiences, Kofi began to feel that the people and institutions that were supposed to protect him had failed. The police hadn't taken his report seriously, and the hospital staff seemed more concerned with paperwork than his well-being. This perceived institutional failure reinforced his feelings of helplessness and low coping ability. Kofi's negative appraisals fed back into his maladaptive strategies; he became even more withdrawn, avoiding conflicts or situations that might trigger another episode of anxiety. His self-blame rumination intensified, making him wonder if he was somehow to blame for the assault. As a result, Kofi started to doubt his own perceptions of safety, constantly second-guessing whether he was truly secure. As the months went by, Kofi's avoidance behaviors took a toll on his relationships and work performance. His colleagues noticed that he was no longer contributing to team meetings, and his girlfriend eventually broke up with him due to his increasing withdrawal. It was only when Kofi realized that he had lost all sense of control over his life that he finally sought help. He hoped therapy could help him break the cycle of self-doubt and fear, but what frightened him most was the prospect of reliving those traumatic memories once again.
